title: Beyond cash: How microenterprise support lifts families out of poverty
gist: World Bank evaluation leaders summarize evidence from Tanzania, Malawi, Ethiopia and Cameroon that economic inclusion programs (cash plus training, coaching and business capital) raise incomes far more than cash alone — Tanzania's PSSN returned $2.99 per $1. Key design lessons: public works add no productive gains, individualized support beats group delivery, credit can substitute for grants for better-off households, and the model works for urban youth with lump-sum grants.

insights.claim: Single interventions such as microfinance, training, cash-for-work and community grants have often failed to produce lasting results, driving interest in economic inclusion programs that combine multiple interventions to address the constraints trapping people in poverty.

insights.so_what: Bundled interventions are now the dominant anti-poverty design paradigm at multilaterals.

insights.claim: Tanzania's Productive Social Safety Net added training, mentoring and business capital grants to cash and public works, increasing household incomes and assets by a third relative to cash transfers alone, with about $2.99 of economic return per $1 invested.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A ~3x return makes economic inclusion among the more cost-effective anti-poverty spends.

insights.claim: In Tanzania, adding public works on top of the livelihoods package produced no additional productive gains, suggesting that what helps households cope is not sufficient to help them grow.

insights.so_what: Governments should separate consumption-smoothing public works budgets from growth-oriented livelihood spending.

insights.claim: Malawi's Social Support for Resilient Livelihoods Project found a more intensive, individualized approach (individual grants) outperformed a cheaper group-based model across food security, consumption, assets, business ownership, revenues and livestock.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Under the individualized model in Malawi, households worked more, became more productive and hired labor to expand their activities.

insights.claim: Ethiopia's Productive Safety Net Program, combining income support with training, coaching and productive capital, generated gains for participants' neighbors as well, suggesting knowledge and behaviors spill over into local economies.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Spillovers imply true program returns exceed participant-only estimates.

insights.claim: For relatively better-positioned participants in Ethiopia, credit often produced impacts comparable to or larger than grants, though repayment and long-term outcomes remain unproven and the poorest may still need subsidies.

insights.claim: Triaging households into those needing grants, those able to use credit productively, and those ready for commercial finance could stretch scarce public grants and open a broader role for markets and private finance in economic inclusion.

themes.theme: Cameroon: urban youth and lump-sum grants

insights.claim: In Cameroon, an economic inclusion model originally designed for poor rural households worked for urban youth: business capital plus training and coaching produced large gains in business activity, revenues, profits, assets, savings and food security.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Expands the addressable population to fast-growing urban youth, a key jobs and stability challenge.
insights.quote: Perhaps the biggest surprise comes from Cameroon.
insights.locator: Cameroon: a rural anti-poverty model works

insights.claim: Cameroon's test found outcomes were essentially the same whether business grants were paid upfront or split into several payments, so the simpler upfront option lowers transactions, delays and administrative costs.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Simplification can cut delivery costs without sacrificing impact.
